cards.heading: Why spanning tree
cards.body: Redundant switch links create layer 2 loops. Ethernet frames have no TTL, so a broadcast would circle forever (a broadcast storm) and MAC tables would flap. Spanning tree blocks just enough ports to leave one loop-free path, and unblocks them if a link fails.

cards.heading: 1. Elect the root bridge
cards.body: Every switch has a bridge ID: priority (default 32768) plus its MAC address. The lowest bridge ID wins: lowest priority, then lowest MAC. PVST+ runs one tree per VLAN and adds the VLAN number to the priority (the extended system ID), so 32768 in VLAN 10 shows as 32778. The low 12 bits of the priority field hold the VLAN ID, so the configurable priority goes in steps of 4096 from 0 to 61440. 'root primary' sets 24576, or 4096 below the current root's priority if that's already lower.
cards.example:
spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 24576   (multiples of 4096)
spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary     (sets 24576 or lower)
cards.mnemonic:
32768 is the middle of the 16-bit range (2^15). Every switch starts in the middle, so you can push one lower to win.
The steps are 4096 because the bottom 12 bits hold the VLAN ID, and 2^12 = 4096. That's why the priority you see is a multiple of 4096 plus the VLAN number: 32768 + 10 = 32778.
In STP, lowest always wins: priority, then MAC, then cost.

cards.heading: 2. Root port on every other switch
cards.body: Each non-root switch picks the one port with the lowest total cost to the root. Default costs: 10 Gbps = 2, 1 Gbps = 4, 100 Mbps = 19, 10 Mbps = 100. Ties go to the lowest neighbour bridge ID, then the lowest neighbour port ID (priority.number). Root path cost adds the cost of every link on the way: two 1 Gbps hops cost 4 + 4 = 8. Tiebreakers in order: lowest root path cost, lowest neighbour bridge ID, lowest neighbour port ID, then lowest local port ID.
cards.example:
SW3 Gi0/1: 0 + 4 = 4   ← root port
SW3 Gi0/2: 4 + 4 = 8
cards.mnemonic:
Count down from the slow end like a launch: 100, 19, 4, 2. That's 10 Mbps, 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps. The faster the link, the lower the cost.
Easy to mix up: these are STP costs. OSPF has its own scale, where 100 Mbps costs 1 by default.

cards.heading: 3. Designated port on every link
cards.body: On each link one end is designated (forwards towards that segment): the end whose switch has the lower root cost, then the lower bridge ID. All the root bridge's ports are designated. Any port that is neither root nor designated becomes an alternate port and blocks (discards).

cards.heading: Rapid PVST+ roles and states
cards.body: Roles: root, designated, alternate (a backup root port) and backup. States: discarding, learning, forwarding. Rapid PVST+ converges in about a second instead of 30-50 seconds for classic STP. An alternate port is a discarding backup path to the root through another switch; a backup port backs up a designated port on the same shared segment (a hub). Root and designated ports forward. RSTP merges 802.1D's disabled, blocking and listening into one discarding state, and converges fast because ports negotiate directly (proposal/agreement) and alternate ports take over immediately.
cards.example:
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
Interface  Role Sts Cost  Prio.Nbr
Gi0/1      Root FWD 4     128.1
Gi0/2      Altn BLK 4     128.2

cards.heading: PortFast and BPDU Guard
cards.body: Access ports to end hosts can skip listening and learning with PortFast. BPDU Guard err-disables a PortFast port if a BPDU arrives, so nobody can plug in a switch and change the tree. An err-disabled port stays down until an admin bounces it (shutdown, no shutdown) or 'errdisable recovery cause bpduguard' brings it back.
cards.example:
interface fa0/5
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable

cards.heading: Root Guard
cards.body: Root Guard protects the root you chose. Put it on designated ports facing switches that must never become root. If a superior BPDU arrives there, the port goes root-inconsistent (blocked) until those BPDUs stop, so a newly connected switch can't take over. BPDU Guard is the edge-port tool: any BPDU err-disables the port.

cards.heading: Classic STP timers and per-VLAN trees
cards.body: Classic 802.1D STP moves a port through blocking (max age 20 s), listening (15 s) and learning (15 s) before forwarding: up to 50 seconds. Running one tree per VLAN (PVST+) lets you make one switch root for some VLANs and another for the rest, so both uplinks carry traffic instead of one sitting blocked.
cards.example:
Blocking -> Listening -> Learning -> Forwarding
  20 s        15 s         15 s
cards.mnemonic:
The states in order: "Bored Lions Learn Fast" (Blocking, Listening, Learning, Forwarding). A port listens for BPDUs before it learns MAC addresses.
Timers: 20 s of max age, then 15 + 15 s of forward delay. 20 + 15 + 15 = 50 s, the classic worst case that Rapid PVST+ was built to avoid.
